Okay so, shipping slow.
My theory, and Theo hates this, is that most teams aren't slow at writing code, they're slow at deciding.
I don't hate it, I just think it's half the story.
Okay, what's the other half?
The other half is that nobody wants to ship something embarrassing, so everything sits in a branch for three weeks getting polished.
Right, the polish trap.
The polish trap, and the worst part is the polish usually goes on stuff users never touch.
Like, we spent a week on the settings page animation last spring.
Oh no, we did, didn't we.
We did, and I checked the analytics, and something like four percent of people ever opened settings.
Four percent!
Four percent, so that's a week of two engineers for a little slide-in effect that almost nobody saw.
Okay, but in fairness, the people who open settings are the power users, and they're the ones who write the angry posts.
That is true, that is very true.
So what do you actually do about it?
The thing that worked for us was a hard rule that anything sitting in review for more than two days gets merged or killed.
Merged or killed, I like that, it's very dramatic.
It's dramatic on purpose, because otherwise everything just lives in this limbo forever.
And did people push back?
Oh, constantly, for like the first month.
Then they kind of noticed they were shipping three times as often and nobody was getting yelled at.
Alright, quick break, and then I want to get into the deciding part.

So, deciding.
Here's my hot take, most meetings that are supposed to make a decision end with a follow-up meeting.
Every single one.
Every single one, and the reason is nobody in the room actually owns the call.
So you get this sort of polite consensus where everyone nods and then nothing happens.
What we started doing, and this is borrowed from a friend at a much bigger company, is one name on every decision.
Not a committee, one person.
And that person is allowed to be wrong.
That's the key part, being wrong has to be allowed, otherwise nobody wants their name on anything.
Do you remember the pricing page thing?
Ugh, yes.
So we went back and forth on pricing for like six weeks.
Six weeks, and in the end Dana just picked a number on a Thursday afternoon.
And it was fine!
It was totally fine, and we changed it two months later anyway.
